How the canyon bends your swell

First Order

The Scripps / La Jolla submarine canyon is a permanent lens carved into the seafloor off San Diego — it decides which beaches a swell hits hard and which it barely reaches. Pick a swell below: the map shows what the canyon alone does to it — red where it makes the surf bigger, blue where it makes it smaller.

The experiment behind the map

Every swell here is simulated twice — over the real seafloor and over a control seafloor with the canyon smoothed away. Left pair: the two seafloors; the canyon is the dark V. Right pair: the wave height each one produces for the swell you have dialled in. Where the two oceans disagree is exactly what the canyon does — that disagreement is the map above.

A phase-resolving Boussinesq wave model (Celeris) run over the real seafloor of the Scripps and La Jolla submarine canyons, and re-run with the canyons filled in. Twenty swells: four periods × five directions, each a full directional-spread sea state; between the five modelled directions the map blends neighbouring runs (a smooth guide, not model output). Colour scales are relative — the model conserves the pattern of focusing, which is what the canyon controls; the map shows the shape of the effect, not a wave-size forecast.

Seafloor: USGS CoNED Southern California 1 m topobathymetric DEM (NOAA Digital Coast).  Land imagery: Esri World Imagery (Esri, Maxar, Earthstar Geographics, and the GIS User Community).  Wave model: Celeris (Lynett et al.), a GPU Boussinesq solver.  Rays: linear-theory wave rays (Snell refraction) traced over the same seafloor — the method first applied to Scripps Canyon by Munk & Traylor (1947).  Companion article at Science of Surfing.
